findings.evidence: "[1P][FACT] A high-frequency English word is often one token (verifiable on most vendor tokenizer demos — e.g. common words like the, we, run render as single tokens)"
findings.issue: Evidence-label mismatch. [1P] is defined as "the model vendor's own spec" with a named source. No specific vendor, model, or tokenizer demo is named; the claim is a general observation verifiable on any tokenizer. The label overstates provenance.
findings.fix_instruction: Downgrade to [2°] or remove the label, and if [1P] is retained, name the specific vendor tokenizer demo being cited.

findings.evidence: "The vLLM FP8-KV blog post's often-quoted '54%' — from its Llama-3.1-8B Table 3 (vLLM blog, post dated 2026-04-22, before the 2026-08-30 evidence cutoff; retrieved 2026-11-15, a post-cutoff access date) [S6]"
findings.issue: The text acknowledges a post-cutoff access date (2026-11-15 vs. cutoff 2026-08-30), but the Preface's access-date rule says a retrieval date later than the cutoff is carried "without a named addendum revision" only where the source's own post date falls inside the cutoff. Here the blog post is dated 2026-04-22, so it is pre-cutoff; the access date is post-cutoff. This is consistent with the rule, but the inline phrasing ("post-cutoff access date") invites confusion with the addendum regime.
findings.fix_instruction: Clarify in the sentence that the source post date is 2026-04-22 (inside the cutoff) and only the access date is post-cutoff, matching the Preface's "access dates are not evidence dates" rule.

findings.evidence: The vLLM FP8-KV blog post's often-quoted '54%' — from its Llama-3.1-8B Table 3 (vLLM blog, post dated 2026-04-22, before the 2026-08-30 evidence cutoff; retrieved 2026-11-15, a post-cutoff access date) [S6] — is, on this book's reading, a decode inter-token-latency (ITL) slope, not a memory ratio or footprint coefficient.
findings.issue: This is a claim about a first-party vendor source's meaning, sourced to [S6] (the References chapter), but it is stated with no in-chapter evidence: no quote from the blog, no table reference beyond 'Llama-3.1-8B Table 3', and no measurement status tag. The book's own evidence rules (Preface, 'Evidence boundary') require that a load-bearing quantitative claim carry Axis 1 + Axis 2 + Axis 3. This paragraph's claim — that a widely quoted number has been misread by the field — carries none of the three tags, and the Preface itself (p. 18) flags 'the access timestamp is carried without a named addendum revision' for exactly this source, which makes the claim's provenance especially sensitive.
findings.fix_instruction: Add a provenance/status tag to the '54%' reading, e.g. '[1P][DERIVED] — the book's reading of [S6] Table 3, not a vendor-stated interpretation; re-verify against the post', and quote the blog's own wording for the 54% figure so the reinterpretation is checkable.

findings.evidence: It is on the order of ~256 KiB (0.26 MB) per token for a 7B-class model (32 layers, d_hidden 4096, full-MHA) and ~1.25 MiB (1.31 MB) per token for a 70B-class model (80 layers, d_hidden 8192, full-MHA) — two reference geometries chosen for the arithmetic, not claims about a specific vendor model
findings.issue: Unit slippage inside a single sentence: '~256 KiB (0.26 MB)' and '~1.25 MiB (1.31 MB)'. 2 × 32 × 4096 × 1 B = 262,144 B = 256 KiB = 0.262 MB ✓, and 2 × 80 × 8192 × 1 B = 1,310,720 B = 1.25 MiB = 1.31072 MB ✓ — the arithmetic is right. But the book's SI convention (stated at Ch. 4, p. 66: 'K = 1,000 and M = 1,000,000 for token counts') and its repeated use of the exact byte counts (2,621,440 B) make '0.26 MB' for 262,144 B and '1.31 MB' for 1,310,720 B consistent. The defect is that Ch. 1 gives both MiB and MB for the same quantity without stating which convention governs the decimal MB figure, while later chapters print 2,621,440 B ≈ 2.62 MB and separately '= 2.5 MiB'. A reader who reads '~1.25 MiB (1.31 MB)' against the canonical FP16 figure of '~2.62 MB' sees a 2× gap that is a precision difference (8-bit vs FP16), and the parenthetical '(1.31 MB)' is at 8-bit while the canonical scenario's KV precision is FP16. The chapter states this later ('The canonical scenario's KV constant is the FP16 figure') but the first mention does not.
findings.fix_instruction: At first mention, add the precision marker inline: '~256 KiB (0.26 MB) per token at 8-bit for a 7B-class model ... ~1.25 MiB (1.31 MB) at 8-bit (~2.62 MB at FP16) for a 70B-class model'. Add one line stating the MiB/MB convention: 'MiB = 2^20 bytes, MB = 10^6 bytes, per the book's SI convention (Ch. 4).'

findings.evidence: A token is the atomic unit of text that a language model reads and writes. It is not necessarily a word, a character, or a byte — it is a vocabulary item, often a byte sequence, chosen by the model's tokenizer.
findings.issue: Scope-claim inconsistency between Ch. 1 and Ch. 3. Ch. 1 scopes itself to 'text-tokenized autoregressive models' and notes that 'Modern multimodal systems also use non-text token-like representations — image patches, audio frames — that are not produced by a text tokenizer'. Ch. 3 §3.1.1 then covers diffusion/LLaDA-style generation where 'the token is not the execution step', and Ch. 2 §2.1.1 covers whole-clip latent video generation where 'frame count, pixel dimensions, latent token count, and model evaluations replace 'output text tokens''. Three chapters scope out non-text or non-AR execution, but Ch. 1's headline definition ('the atomic unit of text that a language model reads and writes') remains unqualified in the book's own summary sentence: 'every downstream cost and capacity number is ultimately a statement about tokens' (p. 22, The Architect's Question) and 'tokens are the interface between a human's request and the machine's arithmetic' (p. 28).
findings.fix_instruction: Qualify the two headline statements with the book's own scope language: 'every downstream cost and capacity number is ultimately a statement about tokens — or, for non-AR generation, about model evaluations (Ch. 3 §3.1.1, Appendix A §9A)'. Add a one-line forward pointer in Ch. 1 to Ch. 2 §2.1.1 and Ch. 3 §3.1.1 so the scoping is visible from the first chapter.

findings.evidence: At 9.2K tokens the canonical FP16 KV per request is ~24.1 GB — 9,200 × 2,621,440 B = 24,117,248,000 B ≈ 24.12 GB — and the 8-bit raw byte-halving variant is ~12.06 GB — 9,200 × 1,310,720 B = 12,058,624,000 B ≈ 12.06 GB, derived from the exact per-token byte count rather than the rounded 1.31 MB constant
findings.issue: Recomputation: 9,200 × 2,621,440 = 24,117,248,000 ✓ (≈24.12 GB) and 9,200 × 1,310,720 = 12,058,624,000 ✓ (≈12.06 GB) — both correct. But Ch. 4's Table 4-2 (p. 88) records the 9.2K residency as '24,117,248,000 B ≈ 24.12 GB (printed ~24.1 GB at one decimal)' while Ch. 1 prints '~24.1 GB' alongside '≈ 24.12 GB' in the same sentence, and Ch. 3 (p. 62) prints '≈ 24.1 GB at FP16 (2.62 MB per token × 9,200 tokens)' while Ch. 7 (p. 141) prints '9,200 ×2.62 MB ≈ 24.1 GB'. Four chapters carry 24.1 / 24.12 for the same quantity and the 9.5K-resident-basis figure carries 24.90 (Ch. 4) vs 24.90368 (Ch. 7). The book's stated convention 'the convention Ch. 7 follows' (Ch. 1, p. 27) is to derive from exact bytes, but Ch. 3 and Ch. 4's tables multiply the rounded 2.62 MB constant instead — the inconsistency the book itself flags in Ch. 1 ('derived from the exact per-token byte count rather than the rounded 1.31 MB constant') is not followed in Ch. 3 or Ch. 4.
findings.fix_instruction: Apply the book's own stated convention uniformly: compute all per-request KV totals from the exact per-token byte count (2,621,440 B) and print one rounded figure per basis (24.12 GB at 9.2K, 24.90 GB at 9.5K). Add the rule to Table 4-2's note: 'Per-context KV totals are derived from 2,621,440 B/token, not from the rounded 2.62 MB constant.'

findings.evidence: 1.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: The Internal Q&A Tool, From First Principles (Chains the continuous scenario — this is its first appearance.)
findings.issue: The chapter's first mini-case states 'this is its first appearance' but Ch. 7 §7.8 (p. 164) and Ch. 8's closing (p. 179ff) present a mini-case about the same 'internal Q&A over internal wikis' for 5,000 employees and Ch. 1 §1.8 also references it. Ch. 7's mini-case heading says 'Sizing Memory First for the 5,000-Employee Wiki' and describes 'We need to let all 5,000 employees ask questions over our internal wikis' — the same ask as Ch. 1's mini-case ('We have thousands of employees who want to ask questions over our internal documents'), with 5,000 vs 'thousands'. The scenarios are therefore not clearly distinguished, and Ch. 7's mini-case opens with 'From the unit-and-token work of Ch 1 alone' and 'The specific sizing ... applies Chapter 4's workload-anatomy method, already developed before this chapter' — a backward reference to a later chapter's method, which reads oddly inside a mini-case framed as the first appearance of the scenario.
findings.fix_instruction: Name the two scenarios distinctly at first appearance: the canonical 2,000-user enterprise Q&A (Ch. 1's first appearance) and the 5,000-employee growth variant (Ch. 4 §4.8, revisited at Ch. 7 §7.8). State at Ch. 1 §1.8: 'a 5,000-employee growth variant of this scenario is worked at Ch. 4 §4.8 and Ch. 7 §7.8'. Remove or rephrase the backward reference to a later chapter's method in Ch. 7's mini-case opening.

findings.evidence:
PDF 17 states: "the two tags are set with no space between them and never break across a line." PDF 27 shows: "[ILLUSTRATIVE]
[DERIVED] Either way, a long context (say 32K tokens) alone can be tens of GB of memory." PDF 29 caption shows: "[ILLUSTRATIVE]
[ASSUMPTION] conceptual"
findings.issue: Evidence-label pairs are visually split across line breaks despite the stated rule that the two tags never break across a line. This weakens the book's own evidence-label discipline and makes inline provenance harder to parse consistently.
findings.fix_instruction: Use a non-breaking space or no-break formatting for every two-tag evidence pair so [PROVENANCE][STATUS] remains on one line. Recheck captions, tables, and prose occurrences where labels wrap.
